p.src: At that moment, Zhou Jin and Yang Zhi reined in their horses beneath the banners and were just about to engage when Wen Da, the Army Supervisor, shouted, “Hold!” He came up to the hall and reported to Secretary Liang: “My lord, although this contest between the two has not yet shown whose skill is superior, spears and swords are merciless weapons, fit only for killing rebels and destroying bandits. Today they are merely competing among our own troops. Should either be injured, the lesser harm would be maiming and the greater death, neither of which would benefit the army. Let the spearheads be removed, the shafts wrapped in felt and dipped in lime on the ground; then have both men mount again wearing black tunics. Let them thrust at each other with the shafts, and whoever bears more white marks shall be the loser.” Secretary Liang said, “Your words are most fitting.” He immediately sent down the order.

p.src: Having received the instructions, the two went behind the drill hall, removed their spearheads, wrapped the ends in felt and bound them into knobs. Each changed into a black tunic, dipped his spear into a tub of lime, mounted again, and rode out before the ranks. Zhou Jin spurred his horse, leveled his spear, and charged straight at Yang Zhi; Yang Zhi likewise urged on his warhorse, twirled the spear in his hand, and met Zhou Jin in combat. Before the ranks the two swept back and forth, round after round, tangled together as though twisted into one mass—rider against rider and horse against horse—for forty or fifty bouts. When they looked at Zhou Jin, he seemed like a slab of tofu that had been knocked over, mottled all across with some thirty or fifty spots. Yang Zhi, by contrast, had only a single white spot beneath his left shoulder blade.

p.src: Secretary Liang was delighted. He summoned Zhou Jin to the hall, examined the marks, and said, “Your former commander appointed you a deputy standard-bearer in the army, but with skill such as yours, how can you campaign north and south? How can you be fit to serve as a salaried deputy standard-bearer?” He ordered Yang Zhi to take over the man’s post. Li Cheng, the Army Supervisor commanding the troops, came up to the hall and reported to Secretary Liang: “Zhou Jin is unpracticed with the spear, but accomplished in archery and horsemanship. If we dismiss him from office merely for this, I fear it may dishearten the army. Why not have Zhou Jin and Yang Zhi compete once more in archery?” Secretary Liang said, “Your words are most fitting.” Another military order was issued, commanding Yang Zhi and Zhou Jin to compete with the bow.

p.src: The two received the order, put away their spears, and each brought out his bow and arrows. Yang Zhi took his bow from its case, fitted it properly, raised it, and sprang onto his horse. Riding before the hall, he halted in the saddle, bent forward, and reported: “My lord, once bow and arrow are loosed, they show no mercy. There may be injury, so I humbly request your command.” Secretary Liang said, “When warriors compete, why fear wounds or maiming? If you possess the skill, you may shoot him dead without blame.” Having received the order, Yang Zhi returned before the ranks. Li Cheng passed down instructions that each of the two archers was to be issued an arrow-shield to protect his body. Each received an arrow-shield and strapped it to his arm. Yang Zhi said, “You shoot three arrows at me first; afterward I shall return three to you.” Hearing this, Zhou Jin longed to shoot an arrow clean through Yang Zhi. Yang Zhi, however, had been trained as a military officer. He saw through Zhou Jin’s methods and thought nothing of him. But how did the two men’s archery contest appear?

p.src: One had shot tigers in the mountains; the other was practiced at piercing a willow leaf through the wind. When their bows were drawn full, hares and foxes lost their lives; When their arrows flew, eagles and ospreys quailed in terror. They matched their arts and contended upon the field; They displayed their methods and won acclaim before the crowd. One knew the wheeling escape, which was truly hard to withstand; The other knew the body-dodging escape, against which no guard availed. Within moments victory and defeat would be seen; in an instant, life and death revealed.

p.src: The blue flag was waved from the command platform. Yang Zhi urged his horse southward, and Zhou Jin galloped after him. Laying his reins across the saddle bow, Zhou Jin held the bow in his left hand, nocked an arrow with his right, drew to the full, and sent it whistling at the center of Yang Zhi’s back. Yang Zhi heard the bowstring sound behind him, instantly swayed aside, and hid his body against the stirrup. The arrow flew harmlessly past. Seeing that his first arrow had missed, Zhou Jin immediately panicked. He hurriedly drew a second arrow from his quiver, nocked it, waited until Yang Zhi was nearer, and shot once more at the center of his back. When Yang Zhi heard the second arrow coming, he did not hide beside the stirrup. The shaft came like the wind, but Yang Zhi had already taken his bow in hand; with a flick of its tip he knocked the arrow spinning down into the grass. When Zhou Jin saw that his second arrow had also missed, he grew more flustered still. Yang Zhi’s horse had already reached the far end of the drill ground. He abruptly wheeled it around, and the horse turned and raced back toward the main hall. Zhou Jin likewise pulled hard on the reins; his horse turned back too, and he followed close in pursuit. Across the lush green turf, the eight hooves flashed like tumbling cups and clashing cymbals, racing with a thunderous clatter like a ball of wind. Zhou Jin took out his third arrow, set it to the string, and drew the bow to the full. Summoning all his strength, he fixed his eyes on the hollow in Yang Zhi’s back and let the arrow fly. Hearing the bowstring sound, Yang Zhi twisted around and, from the saddle, snatched the arrow neatly into his hand. He then galloped before the drill hall and flung down Zhou Jin’s arrow.

p.src: Secretary Liang was overjoyed at the sight. He gave the command for Yang Zhi to shoot three arrows at Zhou Jin in turn. The blue flag was waved again from the command platform. Zhou Jin cast aside his bow and arrows, took the shield in hand, spurred his horse, and rode south. Yang Zhi lifted himself at the waist in the saddle and lightly tapped with his feet; his horse surged forward in pursuit. Yang Zhi first made a feigned draw of his bow. Hearing the bowstring twang behind his head, Zhou Jin twisted around in the saddle and raised his shield to meet the arrow, only to block empty air. Zhou Jin thought, “That fellow only knows how to wield a spear; he cannot shoot a bow. If he feigns again with his second arrow, I shall call a halt and count myself the winner.” Zhou Jin’s horse soon reached the southern end of the drill ground, where it turned back toward the drill hall. When Yang Zhi’s horse saw Zhou Jin’s mount turning back, it too wheeled around. Yang Zhi had already drawn an arrow from his quiver and nocked it to the string. He thought, “If I hit the center of his back, I shall surely take his life. He bears me no grudge, nor I him. I shall merely shoot him somewhere that will not prove fatal.” His left hand seemed to support Mount Tai, his right to cradle an infant; the bow opened like the full moon, and the arrow flew like a meteor. No sooner is it told than done: the arrow struck Zhou Jin squarely in the left shoulder. Caught unprepared, Zhou Jin toppled from his horse. The riderless horse ran straight behind the drill hall. The soldiers hurried off to rescue Zhou Jin. Secretary Liang was delighted. He ordered the Military Administration Office to present the official records at once and had Yang Zhi replace Zhou Jin in his post.

p.src: Condemned in Youyan, he became a banished soldier; before the crowd he fought as though for life itself. With the skill of one whose arrow can pierce a willow leaf, he won the modest honor of a standard-bearer’s post.

p.src: Unexpectedly, a man stepped forward from the left below the stairs and cried, “Do not resign your post! Let the two of us test our skill!” When Yang Zhi looked at him, he saw a man over seven feet tall, with a round face, large ears, broad lips, a square mouth, and a full beard covering his cheeks. Imposing and dignified in appearance, he went straight before Grand Secretary Liang, saluted, and reported, “Zhou Jin has not fully recovered from his illness and was out of spirits; that is why he mistakenly lost to Yang Zhi. Though I am a man of little ability, I wish to match my martial skill against Yang Zhi. If I yield him so much as half an advantage, do not merely remove Zhou Jin and appoint Yang Zhi in his place—give Yang Zhi my own post instead. Even if I die, I shall bear no resentment.” Grand Secretary Liang looked and saw that it was none other than Suo Chao, a regular army officer of the Daming Prefecture Garrison Command. He was so hot-tempered that he flared up like salt thrown into a fire. Always eager to uphold the honor of the state, he strove to distinguish himself and charged first into battle; for this reason everyone called him the “Impetuous Vanguard.” Hearing this, Li Cheng descended from the reviewing platform, went straight to the hall, and reported, “My lord, since this Yang Zhi was once an envoy of the Palace Command, he must possess fine martial skill. Zhou Jin was naturally no match for him. It would be fitting to have him test his martial skill against Officer Suo; then we shall see which is superior.” When Grand Secretary Liang heard this, he thought, “I have been intent on promoting Yang Zhi with all my power, but the officers will not accept it. All the better to let him defeat Suo Chao as well; then they will accept it even at the cost of death and have nothing more to say.”

p.src: Grand Secretary Liang immediately summoned Yang Zhi to the hall and asked, “How would you fare in a trial of martial skill against Suo Chao?” Yang Zhi replied, “How could I dare disobey Your Excellency’s command?” Grand Secretary Liang said, “Since that is so, go behind the hall and change your attire. Arm yourself properly, and have the accompanying officers of the armory issue you the weapons you require. Bring my warhorse as well and lend it to Yang Zhi. Be cautious and attentive; do not take this lightly.” Yang Zhi thanked him and went off to equip himself.

I shall lend them both to you. Be cautious and attentive, and do not let our fighting spirit be broken.” Suo Chao thanked him and likewise went off to equip himself.

p.src: Grand Secretary Liang rose and walked out before the steps. His attendants moved a silver folding chair and set it beside the balustrade of the terrace. Grand Secretary Liang took his seat, with attendants waiting in two rows on either side. He ordered the parasol bearer to open the three-tiered russet gauze sunshade topped with a silver gourd and hold it over him from behind. The command was relayed down from the reviewing platform, and at once the red flag was waved. Gongs and drums sounded together on both sides, beating out one full roll. Within each of the two formations on the drill ground, a cannon was fired. At the cannon blast, Suo Chao galloped into his formation and took cover behind the gate banner. Yang Zhi likewise galloped from his formation into the ranks and went straight behind the gate banner. The yellow flag was waved again upon the reviewing platform, another roll of drums thundered, and both armies raised a single concerted shout. Then no one on the drill ground dared make a sound; all was utterly still. At another clang of the gong, a spotless white flag was raised. None of the officers on either side dared move about or speak out of turn; they stood perfectly still.

p.src: The blue flag was waved upon the reviewing platform. As the third roll of battle drums sounded, the ranks beneath the gate banner of the left formation slowly parted. With the chiming of harness bells, regular officer Suo Chao rode out and came straight before the formation. He reined in his horse and took his weapon in hand—a true hero and champion. He wore a tempered-steel helmet shaped with a lion, behind which rose a red tassel as large as a dipper. His armor was assembled from iron plates, a gilded belt with a beast-faced buckle girded his waist, and bronze heart-guards protected his chest and back. Over it he wore a scarlet robe patterned with roundels of flowers, while two green woolen chin cords hung down from above. On his feet were a pair of slant-cut leather riding boots; a bow hung on his left and a quiver of arrows on his right. Across his hands he held a gold-inlaid battle-axe, and beneath him was Commander Li’s snow-white charger, seasoned in many campaigns. When one looked at the horse, it too was a magnificent steed. Behold: its hue belonged to the western metals, like the white-browed tiger of the Southern Mountains; its coat seemed heaped with lustrous powder, like a jade qilin of the Northern Sea. It could charge through battle lines and leap across streams; it delighted in war drums, yet its nature was noble. It could bear heavy loads and travel far, and was accustomed to neighing into the wind: surely it was a dragon-bred courser. It surpassed Wu Zixu’s Pear-Blossom Horse and outshone the King of Qin’s White-Jade Colt.

If either of you makes any error, he will certainly be punished. But whoever wins shall receive many rich rewards.” Having received the order, the two spurred their horses from the formations and rode to the center of the drill ground. Their mounts crossed, and both kinds of weapon were raised together. Suo Chao, aflame with anger, swung the great axe in his hands and urged his horse forward to fight Yang Zhi. Yang Zhi displayed his might, wielding his marvelous spear as he advanced to meet Suo Chao. p.src: War banners blotted out the sun; murderous fury veiled the heavens. One drove his gold-inlaid axe straight at the crown of the head; the other kept his solid-iron spear fixed upon the heart. This one was Vaisravana, defender of the realm—Li, the Heavenly King Who Bears the Pagoda; That one was the Grand Marshal Tianpeng, who governs the land and commands the Golden Palace. From one man’s spearpoint issued a tongue of flame; from the other’s axe blade burst several shafts of icy light. That one was Yuan Da of the Seven Kingdoms reborn; this one was Zhang Fei of the Three Kingdoms returned to the world. One was the furious Giant Spirit God, brandishing his great axe to split the mountain’s roots; The other was Huaguangzang enraged, wielding his golden spear to pierce open the underworld. This one, stout and imposing, opened his eyes wide and brought his axe chopping down with a crash; That one clenched his teeth with a grinding crack and whirled his spear shaft in fiery arcs as though it would snap. Each watched for an opening, and neither allowed the slightest respite.

p.src: The two fought for more than fifty bouts, with neither gaining the upper hand. On the terrace, Grand Secretary Liang stared in amazement; the assembled officers on both sides watched and cheered without cease; and the soldiers in the ranks looked at one another and said, “We have served in the army for many years and gone on campaign several times, yet when have we ever seen two such heroes fight?” From the commanders’ platform, Li Cheng and Wen Da repeatedly cried, “Splendid fighting!” Wen Da feared that one of them might suffer an internal injury, so he hurriedly summoned the standard-bearer and had him take the command flag and separate them. Suddenly a gong sounded from the commanders’ platform. Yang Zhi and Suo Chao were at the height of the fight, each eager to win the honor, and neither was willing to rein back. The standard-bearer galloped over and called, “You two heroes, cease fighting! His Excellency has given the order.” Only then did Yang Zhi and Suo Chao lower their weapons, rein in their mounts, and gallop back to their respective formations, where they halted beneath their banners. They looked toward Grand Secretary Liang and awaited his command.

p.src: Li Cheng and Wen Da descended from the commanders’ platform, went straight to the foot of the terrace, and reported to Grand Secretary Liang: “Your Excellency, judging by their skills, these two are evenly matched and both deserve important employment.” Grand Secretary Liang was delighted and issued an order summoning Yang Zhi and Suo Chao. The standard-bearer relayed the command and summoned the two men before the hall, where both dismounted. Junior officers took their weapons, and the two entered the hall and bowed to hear the order. Grand Secretary Liang ordered two ingots of silver and two sets of fine cloth to be brought as rewards for them. He then ordered the Military Administration Office to promote both men to military-command intendants, had the appointments entered in the records at once, and received them into office that very day. Suo Chao and Yang Zhi both bowed their thanks to Grand Secretary Liang, carried their rewards down from the hall, laid aside spear, saber, bow, and arrows, removed helmets and armor, and changed their clothes. Suo Chao likewise removed his battle gear and changed into a brocade coat; then both returned to the hall and again bowed their thanks to all the officers. Grand Secretary Liang had Suo Chao and Yang Zhi exchange formal greetings, after which they joined the ranks as intendants. The soldiers beat the drums of victory, took up the gongs, drums, and banners, and dispersed first.

p.src: Grand Secretary Liang and all the officers, high and low, attended a banquet in the martial drill hall. As the red sun sank in the west, the banquet ended. Grand Secretary Liang mounted his horse, and all the officials escorted him back to his residence. The two newly appointed intendants rode at the head of his procession, while mounted attendants flanked them; both men wore red flowers in their caps as they were welcomed through the eastern outer gate. Along both sides of the streets, old people and children alike came out to watch and rejoice. From horseback Grand Secretary Liang asked, “Why are you people so delighted?” The elders all knelt and replied, “We old men were born in Beijing and raised in Daming Prefecture, yet never before today have we seen two such heroic generals test their skills. Having seen such well-matched opponents in the drill ground today, how could we not rejoice?” Grand Secretary Liang was greatly pleased to hear this from horseback. When they returned to the residence, the officials dispersed to their homes. A group of Suo Chao’s comrades invited him away to drink in celebration. Yang Zhi, being newly arrived and knowing no one, went to lodge at the Liang residence, where morning and evening he diligently awaited orders. But no more need be said of this.

p.src: That day Grand Secretary Liang and Lady Cai were holding their family banquet in the rear hall to celebrate the Double Fifth. After several cups of wine and two courses of food, Lady Cai said, “My lord, since entering public life you have risen to command an entire region and bear weighty responsibilities of state. To whom do you owe this rank and wealth?” Grand Secretary Liang replied, “I, Shijie, have studied since childhood and possess some knowledge of the Classics and histories. I am no senseless plant or tree—how could I fail to recognize the favor of my honored father-in-law? I can never be grateful enough for all he has done to advance me!” Lady Cai said, “Since you know the favor my father has shown you, how could you forget his birthday?” Grand Secretary Liang replied, “How could I forget? My honored father-in-law’s birthday is the fifteenth day of the sixth month. I have already had gold, pearls, and precious objects worth one hundred thousand strings of cash purchased to send to the capital in celebration. A month ago, the agents received the funds and began their work. Nine tenths is now ready, and within a few days all will be properly arranged and a man dispatched to set out. There is only one matter over which I hesitate. Last year I purchased many curios, along with gold, pearls, and treasures, and sent men to deliver them; but before they had gone even halfway, bandits robbed them of everything. That whole fortune was squandered in vain, and despite strict efforts to apprehend the bandits, they remain uncaught. Whom should I send this year?” Lady Cai said, “You have many officers and soldiers at your command. Simply choose a trusted man from among them.” Grand Secretary Liang said, “There are still forty or fifty days to go. I shall press them morning and evening until all the gifts are ready; it will not be too late then to choose the man who is to go. You need not concern yourself, my lady. I, Shijie, know how to handle it.” That day’s family banquet lasted from noon until the second watch of the night before it dispersed. Of this no more need be said.

p.src: We shall say no more of Grand Secretary Liang purchasing gifts and curios and choosing someone to go to the capital to celebrate Grand Preceptor Cai’s birthday. Instead, let us tell of the newly appointed magistrate of Yuncheng County in Jizhou, Shandong, whose surname was Shi and given name Wenbin. He was upright and just in office, honest and discerning in his conduct, always compassionate at heart and ever mindful of benevolence. In disputes over fields and land, he first determined right and wrong before taking action; in quarrels and brawls, he weighed the gravity of each offense before passing judgment. In leisure he played the qin and received guests; amid pressing business his swift brush delivered judgments. In name he was the county’s magistrate; in truth he was a father and mother to its people.

p.src: Zhu Tong and Lei Heng were jointly charged with apprehending thieves and bandits. That day, the magistrate summoned them both to the hall. They came forward, saluted, and waited to receive his orders. The magistrate said, “Since taking office, I have heard that bandits have gathered at Liangshan Marsh, in the waterways under the jurisdiction of Jizhou Prefecture, where they plunder the people and resist the government troops. “I also fear that thieves are running rampant through the villages and that evildoers abound. I have summoned you both today so that, sparing yourselves no hardship, you may take the soldiers under your command—one of you going through the west gate and the other through the east—and patrol in separate directions. “If you encounter any bandits, suppress and capture them at once, then report and deliver them to the authorities, but you must not harass the villagers. “I know for a fact that on the hill at Dongxi Village there is a great tree with red leaves, the like of which grows nowhere else. Have your men bring several leaves back and present them at the county office as proof that you truly patrolled that far. “If you return without the red leaves, it will prove that you have deceived me, and I shall punish you without mercy.” The two constables received their orders and returned to their respective quarters. Each mustered the soldiers under his command, and they set out separately on patrol.

p.src: We shall say nothing of Zhu Tong, who led his men through the west gate on patrol, but speak only of Lei Heng. That evening he led twenty soldiers through the east gate and made a circuit of the villages. After covering the whole district, they turned back and came to the hill at Dongxi Village. The men plucked the red leaves and descended into the village. They had gone no more than two or three li when they came to the Temple of the Divine Official. Seeing that the doors of the hall stood open, Lei Heng said, “There is no temple keeper here, yet the doors have been left open. Could some villain be hiding inside? “Let us go straight in and have a look.” The men raised their torches and shone them inside together. There, stretched stark naked upon the altar table, lay a great burly fellow. The weather was hot, and the fellow had rolled some ragged clothes into a bundle for a pillow beneath his neck. There on the altar table he slept soundly, snoring away. Lei Heng looked at him and said, “How strange! How very strange! “His Honor the magistrate is truly divinely perceptive—there really is a bandit here in Dongxi Village!” He let out a great shout. The fellow was just about to struggle when all twenty soldiers rushed forward, bound him with a rope, marched him out through the temple doors, and took him toward the manor of a village headman.
